title: General laws of proembryonic (progenesis), embryonic (embryogenesis) and postembryonic development. Teratogenic factors. Gerontology. Regeneration. Homeostasis. Transplantation

goals.text: To teach the student the periods of ontogenesis, the stages of gametogenesis (spermatogenesis and oogenesis), the types of eggs, the laws of fertilization, cleavage, gastrulation and organogenesis, the mechanisms of ontogenesis, critical periods and teratogenic factors, postnatal development and aging, and the basics of regeneration, transplantation and homeostasis.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the kinds, types and periods of ontogenesis;
the stages of spermatogenesis and oogenesis and the chromosome set and DNA content in them;
the types of eggs by the amount and distribution of yolk and the types of cleavage;
the methods of gastrulation and the derivatives of the germ layers;
embryonic induction, critical periods and teratogens;
the theories of aging, types of regeneration, types of transplantation and the mechanisms of homeostasis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write the genetic formula of the cell at each stage of gametogenesis;
identify the organs that develop from each germ layer;
assess the consequence of a teratogenic effect according to the stage of pregnancy.

blocks.text: **Ontogenesis** (E. Haeckel, 1866) is the individual development of an organism: the set of changes from the formation of the zygote (in asexual reproduction — from separation from the parent) until death. It is **direct** (without a larva — reptiles, birds, mammals) or **indirect** (with metamorphosis — amphibians, insects). Direct development is in turn divided into the **egg-laying** and **intrauterine** types; the intrauterine type is characteristic of humans.

blocks.title: Table 10.1. Periods of human ontogenesis
head: Period
Stages
rows: Fertilization, cleavage, gastrulation, histo- and organogenesis; the embryonic period (up to 8 weeks) and the fetal period (from week 9 until birth)
Newborn period, infancy, childhood, adolescence, maturity, old age, senility and death

blocks.text: **Gametogenesis** is the formation of gametes in the gonads. **Spermatogenesis** proceeds in four stages in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, and **oogenesis** in three stages in the ovary (Figure 10.1).

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Gametogenesis — spermatogenesis and oogenesis: periods of multiplication, growth, maturation and formation; chromosome set and DNA content of the cells at each stage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Stages of spermatogenesis and oogenesis
head: Stage
Spermatogenesis
Oogenesis
Genetic formula
rows: Spermatogonia divide by mitosis (from puberty throughout life)
Oogonia divide by mitosis (only in fetal life)
Primary oocytes (yolk accumulates); arrested in prophase of meiosis I until birth
Meiosis I → secondary spermatocytes (n2c) → meiosis II → spermatids
Meiosis I → secondary oocyte + first polar body; meiosis II (completed at fertilization) → egg + second polar body
1 egg and 3 polar bodies from 1 oogonium

blocks.text: The **spermatozoon** is a motile cell consisting of a head (the nucleus and, in front of it, the enzyme-rich **acrosome**), a neck (centrioles), a middle piece (spirally arranged mitochondria — energy for movement) and a tail (axoneme, 9 + 2). A human spermatozoon is ≈ 60 µm long. The **egg** is immotile and large (≈ 130–150 µm in humans), with nutrients (yolk) in its cytoplasm; it is surrounded by a transparent coat (zona pellucida) and the **corona radiata** made of follicular cells.

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Types of eggs by the amount and distribution of yolk
head: Type
Yolk
Organisms
rows: Moderate, more at the vegetal pole
Very much, occupies the vegetal pole

parts.text: In oogenesis, **dictyotene** is the arrest of primary oocytes in diplotene of meiosis I from birth until ovulation (12–50 years). Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II is completed only when a spermatozoon enters the egg.

blocks.text: **Fertilization** is the fusion of a spermatozoon and an egg forming a diploid **zygote**; in humans it takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Stages: approach of spermatozoa to the egg and the **acrosome reaction** (enzymes dissolve the corona radiata and zona pellucida), entry of one spermatozoon, the **cortical reaction** (blocking entry of other spermatozoa — prevention of polyspermy), and fusion of the male and female pronuclei (syngamy).

**Cleavage** is a series of mitotic divisions of the zygote; the cells formed (**blastomeres**) do not grow and become smaller with each division. The type of cleavage depends on the amount of yolk: **complete (holoblastic)** — equal (lancelet) or unequal (amphibians; asynchronous in humans); **incomplete (meroblastic)** — discoidal (birds, reptiles) or superficial (insects) (Figure 10.2). Cleavage gives a **morula** and then a hollow **blastula**; in mammals it is called a **blastocyst** (trophoblast + embryoblast) and is **implanted** in the uterine wall on day 7.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Types of cleavage: 1 — radial (lancelet, mammals); 2 — spiral (flatworms and annelids, mollusks); 3 — bilateral (ascarids); 4 — anarchic; on the right — holoblastic, discoidal and superficial cleavage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Gastrulation** is the formation of a two- and then three-layered embryo — the **gastrula** — from the single-layered blastula; the **germ layers** — **ectoderm**, **endoderm** and **mesoderm** — are formed (Figure 10.3). Methods: **invagination** (infolding — lancelet), **immigration** (migration of cells inward), **delamination** (splitting into layers) and **epiboly** (overgrowth — amphibians). Then **neurulation** (formation of the neural tube and notochord) and **histo-organogenesis** begin.

blocks.label: Figure 10.3
blocks.caption: Stages of embryonic development — cleavage, gastrulation and histo-organogenesis: 1 — blastocoel; 2 — blastopore; 3 — ectoderm; 4 — endoderm; 5 — mesoderm; 6 — neural tube; 7 — notochord; 8 — primitive gut (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 10.4. Derivatives of the germ layers
head: Layer
Tissues and organs formed
rows: Epidermis and its derivatives (hair, nails, sweat and mammary glands), nervous system, receptors of the sense organs, lens of the eye, tooth enamel, epithelium of the oral and anal cavities, anterior pituitary, adrenal medulla
Epithelium of the digestive tube (middle part) and airways, liver, pancreas, epithelium of the thyroid, parathyroid glands and thymus, epithelium of the urinary bladder
Skeleton, striated and smooth muscles, connective tissue, heart and blood vessels, blood, kidneys, gonads, adrenal cortex, serous membranes

sections.title: 4. Mechanisms of ontogenesis, critical periods and teratogenic factors

blocks.text: In ontogenesis cells **divide, migrate, differentiate** and **die** (apoptosis). Early blastomeres are **totipotent** — each can give rise to a whole organism (identical twins arise on this basis). **Differentiation** is the structural and functional specialization of cells with the same genotype as a result of activation of different genes. **Embryonic induction** (H. Spemann, 1924) is the determination of the developmental fate of one part of the embryo by another part (the inducer, for example chordamesoderm) (formation of the neural tube from ectoderm).

**Critical periods** are the periods when the embryo is most sensitive to harmful factors (P.G. Svetlov): the period of **implantation** (weeks 1–2 — harmful effects follow the “all or nothing” principle: the embryo dies or recovers completely) and the period of **organogenesis** (weeks 3–8 — severe congenital defects), as well as the period of **placentation**. In the fetal period harmful effects mainly cause functional disorders and growth retardation.

blocks.title: Table 10.5. Teratogenic factors
head: Group
Examples
Consequences
rows: Thalidomide, retinoids, warfarin, valproate, alcohol, nicotine, heavy metals (mercury, lead)
Phocomelia (thalidomide), fetal alcohol syndrome, neural tube defects
Deafness, cataract, heart defects (rubella), hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis (toxoplasmosis)
Heart and skeletal defects, intellectual disability, cretinism

parts.text: When planning a pregnancy, taking **folic acid** (3 months before pregnancy and in the first trimester) markedly reduces the risk of neural tube defects; alcohol, smoking and taking drugs without a doctor’s advice are forbidden in pregnancy, and vaccination against rubella is given before pregnancy.

blocks.text: In postnatal development the organism grows, organs mature and puberty occurs. Growth and development are controlled by the **genotype**, **hormones** (growth hormone, thyroxine, sex hormones, insulin) and **environmental** factors (nutrition, physical activity, social conditions). The biological age of the organism is assessed by the skeleton, teeth, sexual maturation and other indicators and may differ from the chronological age (acceleration and retardation).

**Aging** is a natural process in which the adaptive capacity of the organism gradually decreases and the probability of disease and death increases. Aging and old age are studied by **gerontology**, and the diseases of the elderly and their treatment by **geriatrics**.

blocks.title: Table 10.6. Main theories of aging
head: Theory
Essence
rows: Human fibroblasts divide only ≈ 50 times in culture; telomeres shorten with each division
Reactive oxygen species damage DNA, proteins and membranes; the damage accumulates
Mutations accumulate in somatic cells and impair cell function
Age-related changes in the hypothalamus and endocrine regulation
Weakening of immunity and strengthening of autoimmune reactions

blocks.text: **Progeria** is a hereditary disease with premature aging: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria in children (mutation of the lamin A gene) and Werner syndrome in adults (a DNA helicase gene). **Death** is the cessation of the vital activity of the organism: **clinical death** (breathing and heart activity have stopped, but recovery by resuscitation is possible within 5–6 minutes) and **biological death** (irreversible changes, first of all in the cerebral cortex).

**Regeneration** is the restoration of lost or damaged parts of the organism. **Physiological regeneration** is the renewal of worn-out cells in the normal course of life (epidermis, intestinal epithelium, blood cells). **Reparative regeneration** is restoration after injury: **complete** (restitution — the original tissue is restored) and **incomplete** (substitution — a scar forms). Methods: epimorphosis (growth from the wound surface), morphallaxis (rebuilding of the remaining part), regenerative hypertrophy (in the liver and kidney — the volume of the organ is restored, but not its shape). The capacity for regeneration decreases in the course of evolution and with age.

blocks.title: Table 10.7. Types of transplantation
head: Type
Donor and recipient
Result
rows: The same organism (from oneself to oneself — skin, bone)
Genetically different individuals of the same species
Rejected if HLA does not match; immunosuppression needed
Different species (for example, from a pig to a human)

blocks.text: Graft rejection is the response of the recipient’s immune system to the donor’s foreign **HLA antigens** (histocompatibility antigens, on chromosome 6). To prevent rejection, the donor is selected by HLA and immunosuppressants are used. Avascular tissues such as the cornea and cartilage are rarely rejected.

**Homeostasis** (W. Cannon, 1929) is the ability of the organism to keep its internal environment (temperature, pH, osmotic pressure, glucose and ion levels) relatively constant. It is maintained at the **genetic** (stability of genotype and karyotype — DNA repair), **structural** (preservation of the composition of cells and tissues — regeneration) and **physiological** levels by the nervous, endocrine and immune systems on the principle of **feedback**.

After meiosis II write the spermatid, spermatozoon and egg as 1n1c.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans 4 spermatozoa are formed from one spermatogonium during spermatogenesis.
cases.ask: How many stages does spermatogenesis have? At which stage are spermatozoa formed? What are their chromosome set and DNA content?
cases.answer: Spermatogenesis has 4 stages: multiplication (spermatogonia, 2n2c), growth (primary spermatocyte, 2n4c), maturation (meiosis I — secondary spermatocytes n2c, meiosis II — spermatids 1n1c) and formation (spermiogenesis — spermatozoa from spermatids). Spermatozoa are formed at the formation stage; they are haploid — 1n1c (in humans 23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes + X or Y).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In human oogenesis one egg is formed from one oogonium at the maturation stage.
cases.ask: What stages does oogenesis have? What other cells are formed at the maturation stage, and what process is this stage related to?
cases.answer: Oogenesis has 3 stages: multiplication (completed in fetal life), growth and maturation. In maturation, meiosis I gives a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, and meiosis II gives the egg and the second polar body; in total 1 egg and 3 polar bodies (the cytoplasm is divided unequally and nutrients accumulate in the egg). Maturation is related to monthly ovulation after puberty: meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II at fertilization.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In week 5 of pregnancy a woman took a drug for a long time without medical supervision, and later heart and limb defects were found in the fetus. Another woman took the same drug in week 30 of pregnancy, but no defects were found.
cases.ask: Explain the difference in the results.
cases.answer: Week 5 falls in the critical period of organogenesis (weeks 3–8): in this period the organ primordia are formed, and a teratogenic effect leads to severe anatomical defects. By week 30 the organs are already formed (fetal period), so a teratogenic effect may cause mainly functional disorders and growth retardation rather than major defects. The consequence of a teratogenic effect depends on the type of substance, its dose and the stage of pregnancy.

cards.back: Individual development from the zygote to death (E. Haeckel)
3 stages; 1 egg + 3 polar bodies from 1 oogonium
Arrest of oocytes in diplotene of meiosis I for years
Very little yolk (humans, mammals); complete cleavage
Formation of three germ layers: ecto-, endo-, mesoderm
One part determines the development of another part (Spemann)
A human cell divides ≈ 50 times; telomeres shorten
Different individuals of the same species; HLA matching and immunosuppression needed

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Spermatogenesis: **4 stages → 4 gametes**; oogenesis: **3 stages → 1 gamete + 3 bodies**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Germ layers: **“Ecto — Ears and Thinking”** (nerves, senses, skin), **“Endo — Eating and Breathing inside”** (digestive and respiratory epithelium), **“Meso — Muscles and Heart”** (muscle, skeleton, blood).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Weeks 3–8 are the critical period of organogenesis: in this period drugs, alcohol, radiation and infections cause the most severe congenital defects.
